newsitem.title: FRANCE: No comment on failed quest for Cr Lyonnais buyer.
newsitem.headline: No comment on failed quest for Cr Lyonnais buyer.

text.p: U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs, advisor to the French government on Credit Lyonnais, would not comment on Thursday on a report it came up empty handed in a quest for potential buyers for the ailing state-owned bank.

But banking analysts said the report in the Financial Times newspaper was no surprise. Bank chairman Jean Peyrelevade "has been saying for weeks the bank will need a couple of years to put things right and then it can be sold", said one analyst.

The newpspaper said Goldman Sachs contacted a number of big European banks, including Britain's Barclays Plc, as well as financial institutions, to see whether they were interested in the bank. But it had been told the bank was unsaleable in its current state, the newspaper reported.
The finance ministry also would not comment.
Goldman Sachs was named earlier this year by the ministry to "help it to look at strategic opportunities" for the bank, a person close to the dossier said.

The banks approached were believed to have said they would only consider buying Credit Lyonnais if they were free to cut its domestic branch network and make many staff redundant, the newspaper said. Such moves would meet stiff union resistance.
Finance minister Jean Arthuis said in September the government was open to offers for a majority or a minority stake in the bank.

But Peyrelevade, chairman of the bank, repeated in a newspaper interview on Friday that while the bank's viability was assured, "it will need two years to put Credit Lyonnais in a state to be privatised".
The bank, brought to the edge of collapse by a hectic expansion spree in the late 1980s and early 1990s, reported a modest first half profit of 67 million francs.

The bank, already bailed out twice by the government, has said it would need to be recapitalised to boost its solvency ratios before being sold and the government has said it plans to put together another aid package for the bank.
Its takeover by a bank or financial institution whose balance sheet was stronger might alleviate the government's need to inject new funds into Credit Lyonnais before selling it.
But analysts said the weak banking climate in France with its low margins resulting from fierce competition would discourage foreign buyers.
"There's no really good reason for a foreign bank to be interested in buying Credit Lyonnais," said one Paris analyst. "There really aren't any examples of any having much success."
German insurer Allianz AG, whose products are already being sold over Credit Lyonnais's counters, on Wednesday denied a report that it was interested in taking over the bank.
The report said the price would be a symbolic one French franc on the grounds thta Credit Lyonnais's valuation would be adjusted to account for its need to be recapitalised.
